L7@P0: The microtype package provides a LaTeX interface to the micro-typographic extensions that were introduced by pdfTeX and some of which have since also propagated
L8@P0: to LuaTeX and XeTeXXeTeX : most prominently, character protrusion and font expansion,
L9@P0: furthermore the adjustment of interword spacing and additional kerning, as well as
L10@P0: hyphenatable letterspacing (tracking) and the possibility to disable all or selected
L11@P0: ligatures. These features may be applied to customisable sets of fonts, and all microtypographic aspects of the fonts can be configured in a straight-forward and flexible
L12@P0: way. Settings for various fonts are provided.
L13@P0: Note that character protrusion requires pdfTeX (version 0.14f or later), LuaTeX ,
L14@P0: or XeTeXXeTeX (at least version 0.9997). Font expansion works with pdfTeX (version 1.20
L15@P0: for automatic expansion) or LuaTeX . The package will by default enable protrusion
L16@P0: and expansion if they can safely be assumed to work. Disabling ligatures requires
L17@P0: pdfTeX (≥ 1.30) or LuaTeX , while the adjustment of interword spacing and of kerning
L18@P0: only works with pdfTeX (≥ 1.40). Letterspacing is available with pdfTeX (≥ 1.40),
L19@P0: LuaTeX (≥ 0.62) or XeTeXXeTeX .
L20@P0: The alternative package letterspace, which also works with plain TeX , provides
L21@P0: the user commands for letterspacing only, omitting support for all other extensions
L22@P0: (see section 7).

L61@P2: 1 Micro-typography with TeX
L62@P2: Micro-typography is the art of enhancing the appearance and readability of a
L63@P2: document while exhibiting a minimum degree of visual obtrusion. It is concerned
L64@P2: with what happens between or at the margins of characters, words or lines. Whereas
L65@P2: the macro-typographical aspects of a document (i.e., its layout) are clearly visible
L66@P2: even to the untrained eye, micro-typographical refinements should ideally not even
L67@P2: be recognisable. That is, you may think that a document looks beautiful, but you
L68@P2: might not be able to tell exactly why: good micro-typographic practice tries to
L69@P2: reduce all potential irritations that might disturb a reader.
L70@P2: Some essential micro-typographical aspects are already taken care of by TeX out
L71@P2: of the box – and in an outstanding manner – namely, hyphenation and justification,
L72@P2: as well as kerning and ligatures. Other aspects are in the user’s scope of responsibilities, e.g., to specify the right amounts of spacing around punctuation characters,
L73@P2: numbers, or quotation marks. On top of this, a number of long-standing microtypographic techniques have been introduced to the TeX world relatively recently
L74@P2: with pdfTeX , and have since also propagated to LuaTeX and XeTeXXeTeX . These features
L75@P2: make them the tool of choice not only for the creation of electronic documents
L76@P2: but also of works of outstanding time-honoured typography: most prominently,
L77@P2: character protrusion (also known as margin kerning) and font expansion. Quoting
L78@P2: Hàn Thê´ Thành, the author of pdfTeX , who writes in his thesis:
L79@P2: After you have read the text

L88@P2: ‘Margin kerning is the adjustments of the characters at the margins of a typeset text.
L89@P2: A simplified employment of margin kerning is hanging punctuation. Margin kerning
L90@P2: is needed for optical alignment of the margins of a typeset text, because mechanical
L91@P2: justification of the margins makes them look rather ragged. Some characters can
L92@P2: make a line appear shorter to the human eye than others. Shifting such characters
L93@P2: by an appropriate amount into the margins would greatly improve the appearance
L94@P2: of a typeset text.
L95@P2: Composing with font expansion is the method to use a wider or narrower variant
L96@P2: of a font to make interword spacing more even. A font in a loose line can be substituted by a wider variant so the interword spaces are stretched by a smaller amount.
L97@P2: Similarly, a font in a tight line can be replaced by a narrower variant to reduce
L98@P2: the amount that the interword spaces are shrunk by. There is certainly a potential
L99@P2: danger of font distortion when using such manipulations, thus they must be used
L100@P2: with extreme care. The potentiality to adjust a line width by font expansion can be
L101@P2: taken into consideration while a paragraph is being broken into lines, in order to
L102@P2: choose better breakpoints.’ [Thành 2000, p. 323]

L157@P2: Another micro-typographic technique, which has always been extremely difficult
L158@P2: to achieve in TeX , is robust and hyphenatable letterspacing (tracking). 1 Whereas
L159@P2: letterspacing can easily be, and often is, abused when applying it to lowercase
L160@P2: letters, readability may be increased by slightly letterspacing (small) capitals or by
L161@P2: decreasing the tracking of very large uppercase type.
